204.title: The body is the field (13.1–13.6)
204.hook: the Gita began on a battlefield; chapter thirteen says the real field is you
204.howItsDone: Hindu teachers often use Gita 13's field and knower of the field (kshetra and kshetrajna) in meditation and study, as a way of noticing the body and mind as something known, and asking who the knower is.

segments.voice: Yesterday: priya, the one dear to me. A portrait of the devoted person, and your line, free from hate, friendly to all. Did someone leave you lighter? Today, a new chapter, and a new picture. Day two hundred four.

Go all the way back to the first line of the Gita. The blind king Dhritarashtra asks: on the field of dharma, the field of the Kurus, what did my sons and the sons of Pandu do? Dharmakshetre, kurukshetre. The whole book opens on a field. Two armies, dust, chariots, a man about to break down. Twelve chapters later, chapter thirteen picks up that same word, field, kshetra, and turns it around. The field, Krishna says, isn't only out there where the armies stand. You're standing in it. You are it.
screen: `ON THE FIELD OF DHARMA.` → `TWO ARMIES, ONE FIELD.` → `THE FIELD IS YOU.`

segments.voice: Chapter thirteen opens with a definition. This body, Arjuna, is called the field. And the one who knows it, the sages call the knower of the field. Kshetra, the field. Kshetrajna, the knower of the field. Think of a farmer's field. Things grow there, weeds and wheat. Weather passes over it. Seasons change it. And standing at the edge is someone who watches it and knows it, who isn't the dirt. Then Krishna adds the line that makes this chapter famous: know me also as the knower of the field in all fields. The same knower, in every body. Hindu schools read that line differently. Advaita teachers say the knower in you and the divine knower are finally one. Ramanuja and the Vaishnava schools say the divine dwells in every knower as its inner guide, close but not identical. Both read it from the same verse. Then verses five and six list what's in the field, and the list is bigger than you'd guess. The elements. The sense of I. The intellect. The senses and the mind, and what they reach for. And then this: desire, aversion, pleasure, pain, the body as a whole, awareness, steadiness. Your wanting, your not wanting, even your moods: all field. All things that grow and change and pass. Here's why that matters on an ordinary Tuesday. When anger comes up, the Gita's picture says: something is growing in the field. You can notice it from the edge. You are not only the weather. That's the word today: the body is the field.
screen: `THIS BODY IS CALLED THE FIELD.` · `THE KNOWER OF THE FIELD.` · `THE KNOWER IN ALL FIELDS.` · `EVEN DESIRE AND PAIN ARE FIELD.` · then, large: `THE BODY IS THE FIELD.`

segments.voice: Sit, and walk the edge of your own field. Notice the body first: its weight, its warmth, the places that ache. That's field. Notice the breath coming and going. Field. Notice a thought arrive, maybe a worry, maybe a wish. Field too. Then, for a moment, notice the one noticing. You don't have to name it. Just stand at the edge and watch things grow and pass. The bell holds the time.
Kshetra, the field. Gita thirteen: the body, with its senses, desires and moods, is the field; the one who knows it is the knower of the field, kshetrajna.
Your line: the field. Today, when a strong feeling rises, say quietly to yourself: the field. Something is growing. Then watch it from the edge for one breath. Day two hundred four.

205.title: Knowledge and its opposite (13.7–13.18)
205.hook: the Gita's list of what knowledge is starts with something you can't look up
205.howItsDone: Hindu teachers often quote Gita 13.7–13.11 as a checklist of character for students, starting with amanitva, humility; many traditions treat serving and honoring the teacher as part of this knowledge.

segments.voice: Yesterday: kshetra, the body is the field, and there's a knower at its edge. Your line was the field. Did you catch something growing there? Today, what the knower actually knows. Day two hundred five.

The smartest person at a dinner table might have three degrees and win every argument. The wisest person at that table is often someone else. The wise one might have no degree at all. They just listen longer, and they don't need to be right. The Gita has noticed this too. In chapter thirteen Krishna gives a list with the heading knowledge. You'd expect facts, or philosophy, or a curriculum. Instead the list opens with something no exam can test.
screen: `THE SMARTEST AT THE TABLE.` → `THE WISEST AT THE TABLE.` → `NOT ALWAYS THE SAME.`

segments.voice: Verse seven. The first word on the list is amanitva: humility, not thinking much of yourself. Then adambhitva, no pretending. Then ahimsa, doing no harm, a word you met in camp one. Then patience, straightforwardness, serving your teacher, cleanliness, steadiness, self-control. The list keeps going. Not being dragged by the senses. Not being ruled by the sense of I. Seeing clearly that birth, age, sickness and death bring pain. Not clinging too tightly to home and family. Staying even when things go well and when they don't. Steady devotion. A taste for quiet places, and less need for the crowd. A long list, and Krishna ends with a surprise. This, he says, is called knowledge. And whatever is the opposite of this is ajnana, ignorance. So in the Gita, knowledge isn't only what's in your head. It's what shows in how you live. A brilliant, arrogant person, by this definition, is missing the first item. Then from verse twelve the chapter turns to what is to be known, Brahman, and the description goes strange on purpose. It has hands and feet everywhere, eyes and faces everywhere. It shines through every sense, yet has no senses. It's far away, and it's near. It's inside beings and outside them. It seems divided among beings, yet it's undivided. Verse seventeen calls it the light of lights, beyond darkness. The words are stretching to point at something words can't hold. And the door to it, the list says, starts with humility. That's the word today: knowledge and its opposite.
screen: `FIRST ON THE LIST: HUMILITY.` · `KNOWLEDGE IS HOW YOU LIVE.` · `THE OPPOSITE IS IGNORANCE.` · `FAR AND NEAR, THE LIGHT OF LIGHTS.` · then, large: `KNOWLEDGE AND ITS OPPOSITE.`

segments.voice: Sit, and think of a recent moment you needed to be right. A text thread, a meeting, a family dinner. Don't judge it. Just see it. Now picture that same moment, and let the need drop by one notch. Maybe you ask a question instead of making a point. Maybe you simply listen. Breathe into that softer version. Notice how it feels in the chest. That softness is the first item on the Gita's list. The bell holds the time.
Amanitva, humility, not thinking much of yourself. Gita thirteen, seven to eighteen: knowledge is a way of living that begins with it, and its opposite is ignorance.
Your line: humility first. Today, in one conversation, let someone else be right, or ask one real question before you answer. Day two hundred five.

206.title: Seeing the same in all (13.19–13.34)
206.hook: one sun lights the whole world; chapter thirteen says one knower lights every field
206.howItsDone: Many Hindus greet others with namaste, often explained as honoring the divine in the other person; Gita 13.27–13.28, seeing the same Lord in all beings, is one of the verses teachers point to for this.

segments.voice: Yesterday: amanitva, knowledge and its opposite. A list of how to live, and the first item was humility. Your line was humility first. Did you let someone else be right? Today, the chapter's last and biggest picture. Day two hundred six.

Noon light falls on a whole street: the parked cars, the dog on the corner, the neighbor nobody gets along with, the trash can, the rose bush. All of it, at once, the same light. The sun doesn't choose. It doesn't get dirty from shining on the trash, and it doesn't get prettier from shining on the roses. Chapter thirteen ends with that exact picture. It's the Gita's answer to a question it has been circling all chapter: who is the knower of the field?
screen: `NOON LIGHT ON A WHOLE STREET.` → `THE ROSE AND THE TRASH CAN.` → `THE SAME LIGHT ON BOTH.`

segments.voice: First, two words the Gita uses a lot from here on. Prakriti: nature, everything that moves and changes, the body, the senses, the mind. Purusha: the person, the conscious one who experiences it. Verse twenty: nature is behind all doing, and the person is behind the experiencing of pleasure and pain. Then verse twenty-seven, the center of today. The one who sees the supreme Lord standing the same in all beings, not perishing when they perish, that one truly sees. Verse twenty-eight follows it: samam pashyan, seeing the same Lord everywhere, such a person doesn't harm the self by the self. Commentators unpack that line in more than one way. Some readers hear in it: if the same one lives in everyone, hurting another is hurting yourself. Verse twenty-nine adds: the one who sees that nature does the acting, and that the self is not the doer, sees. Then two pictures to close the chapter. Verse thirty-two: space is everywhere, and because it's so subtle, it's never stained by what it holds. So the self in every body is never stained. And verse thirty-three: as the one sun lights up this whole world, so the knower of the field lights up the whole field. One light, many fields. The schools differ again on how literally to take the oneness: Advaita as one self, Vaishnava schools as one Lord dwelling in many selves. Either way, the verse asks for one kind of seeing: look at anyone, and look for the light. That's the word today: seeing the same in all.
screen: `NATURE ACTS. THE PERSON KNOWS.` · `THE SAME LORD IN ALL BEINGS.` · `HARM NONE, HARM NOT YOURSELF.` · `ONE SUN LIGHTS THE WHOLE WORLD.` · then, large: `SEEING THE SAME IN ALL.`

segments.voice: Sit, and picture a light at your center, steady and warm. Now picture the person nearest you right now, in the next room or the next house. Picture the same light in them. Then someone across town. Then someone on the other side of the world whose name you'll never know. Then, if you're willing, someone you find hard. Same light. You don't have to like them. Just see the light. The bell holds the time.
Sama, the same, even. Gita thirteen, twenty-seven: the one who sees the same Lord standing in all beings, imperishable in the perishing, truly sees.
Your line: the one light. Today, pick three strangers, a driver, a clerk, someone in line, and silently notice the same light in each. Day two hundred six.

207.title: Sattva, rajas, tamas (14.1–14.9)
207.hook: three threads run through everything in nature, and through every mood you've had
207.howItsDone: The three gunas are part of Hindu vocabulary: some people describe foods, habits, music and moods as sattvic, rajasic or tamasic, and Ayurveda and yoga teachers use the terms too.

segments.voice: Yesterday: sama, seeing the same in all. One sun lights the whole world, one knower lights every field. Your line was the one light. Did you see it in a stranger? Today, what the field is woven from. Day two hundred seven.

Six in the morning: heavy, foggy, begging for ten more minutes. Ten o'clock: wired, three tabs open, answering messages on the walk to the next thing. And once in a while, around sunset, a clear, quiet moment when everything seems simple and bright. Same person. Three completely different weathers. Hindu thought has names for those three weathers, and it says they aren't only in people. They're in food, in music, in the whole of nature. Chapter fourteen is where the Gita lays them out.
screen: `FOGGY AT SIX.` → `WIRED AT TEN.` → `CLEAR AT SUNSET.`

segments.voice: Verse five. Sattva, rajas, tamas: these gunas, born of nature, bind the undying one in the body. The word guna means a quality, and in ordinary Sanskrit it can also mean a strand or a thread, even the cord of a bowstring. So picture a rope of three strands, twisted together. Everything in nature is made of all three, in different mixes. Now each one. Sattva is clarity, brightness, balance. Verse six: it's clear and it lights things up, and it's free of trouble. But even sattva binds, the Gita says, by attachment to happiness and to knowledge. You can get hooked on feeling good and feeling wise. Rajas is passion, motion, heat. Verse seven: it comes from craving and attachment, and it binds by attachment to action. It's the part of you that can't stop doing. Tamas is darkness, heaviness, inertia. Verse eight: it's born of ignorance and it deludes. It binds through carelessness, laziness and sleep. Verse nine sums it up: sattva ties you to happiness, rajas to action, tamas covers over understanding and ties you to heedlessness. Two things follow from these verses. First, none of the three is simply the good one. Even the bright thread is still a thread. Second, some teachers stress that this is a description, not a verdict: rest needs a little tamas, and getting out of bed needs a little rajas. The point isn't to hate any strand. It's to see the rope. Our word today is the first and clearest of the three: sattva.
screen: `GUNA: A QUALITY, A THREAD.` · `SATTVA: CLEAR AND BRIGHT.` · `RAJAS: PASSION AND MOTION.` · `TAMAS: HEAVY AND DARK.` · then, large: `SATTVA.`

segments.voice: Sit, and check your own rope right now. Is there heaviness, a pull toward sleep or blankness? That's the dark thread. Is there buzzing, a list running, a wish to get up and do something? That's the moving thread. Is there any clarity, even a little, a moment of simply seeing? That's the bright one. Don't pick a favorite. Just notice the mix, the way you'd notice the weather. The bell holds the time.
Sattva. Clarity, brightness, balance: the first of the three gunas, the strands of nature, with rajas, motion, and tamas, heaviness.
Your line: three threads. Today, at three different moments, morning, midday and evening, name which thread is strongest right then. Day two hundred seven.

208.title: How they show up (14.10–14.20)
208.hook: the Gita gives field signs for each of the three threads
208.howItsDone: Some Hindus use the gunas as a practical check on daily life, choosing food, company and routines that support sattva; some teachers use Gita 14.11–14.13 to describe what each guna looks like.

segments.voice: Yesterday: sattva, rajas, tamas. Clarity, motion, heaviness, twisted together like a rope. Your line was three threads. Which one was strongest at midday? Today, how to spot each one. Day two hundred eight.

Birdwatchers don't need to see the whole bird. A flash of red on the wing, a certain call at dawn, the way it flies in loops, and they know. They call those field marks. Chapter fourteen does the same thing for the three gunas. Yesterday we met them in theory. Today Krishna gives the field marks: what each one looks like when it's winning, in a person, in a room, maybe in you this afternoon. It reads almost like a checklist.
screen: `A FLASH OF RED, A CALL AT DAWN.` → `FIELD MARKS.` → `FOR THE THREE THREADS.`

segments.voice: Verse ten starts with a rule: one thread rises by pushing down the other two. Sattva comes up by overpowering rajas and tamas. Rajas by overpowering sattva and tamas. And tamas by overpowering the other two. The mix is always shifting. Then the field marks. Verse eleven: when light and understanding shine through every gate of the body, the eyes, the ears, the mind, then sattva is strong. Verse twelve: greed, busyness, starting one project after another, restlessness, longing. That's rajas rising. Verse thirteen: darkness, sluggishness, carelessness, confusion. That's tamas. Then the Gita follows each thread to where it leads. Verse seventeen: from sattva comes knowledge. From rajas comes greed. From tamas come carelessness, confusion, and not knowing. Verse eighteen gives a picture of direction: those in sattva rise, those in rajas stay in the middle, those in tamas sink. And the chapter even says the thread you're in at the end of life shapes what comes next. But the turn comes in verse nineteen. When the seer sees that there is no doer other than the gunas, and knows what is beyond them, that one reaches my being. In other words: it's the threads that are moving. The one watching isn't a thread. That's why noticing matters so much. The moment you can say, oh, that's rajas, you're already standing a little outside it. That's the word today: how they show up.
screen: `ONE RISES, TWO FALL.` · `LIGHT, GREED, OR FOG.` · `KNOWLEDGE, GREED, CONFUSION.` · `THE SEER SEES THE THREADS MOVE.` · then, large: `HOW THEY SHOW UP.`

segments.voice: Sit, and scan for field marks. Check the eyes and ears: is there light coming through, a clear seeing? Check the chest and hands: is there restlessness, wanting, a pull to start something? Check the head: is there fog, heaviness, a wish to go blank? Whatever is strongest, name it softly: that's the bright thread, or the moving one, or the heavy one. Then rest as the one who noticed. The bell holds the time.
Rajas, passion, motion, heat. Gita fourteen, ten to twenty: light through every gate is sattva, greed and restlessness are rajas, fog and carelessness are tamas, and the seer watches them move.
Your line: notice yours today. Before one decision today, even a small one, check which thread is strongest. Then decide. Day two hundred eight.

209.title: Beyond the three (14.21–14.27)
209.hook: Arjuna asks what a person beyond the three threads looks like
209.carry: the same in praise and blame
209.howItsDone: Hindu teachers hold up the gunatita of Gita 14.22–14.25 as a picture of spiritual maturity; many devotional traditions point to 14.26, unwavering devotion, as the way there.

segments.voice: Yesterday: rajas, how they show up. Light through the gates, greed and restlessness, fog. Your line was notice yours today. Did you catch a thread before a decision? Today, the one who isn't pulled by any of them. Day two hundred nine.

Post something online and watch what happens to you. A hundred likes, and you feel tall. One cruel comment, and it rattles around your head all night. The hundred don't cancel out the one. Most of us are built this way: praise lifts us, blame drops us, and we spend a lot of energy managing both. At the end of chapter fourteen, Arjuna asks a very practical question. What does someone look like who has gone beyond the three threads? How do they act? How do they get there?
screen: `A HUNDRED LIKES.` → `ONE CRUEL COMMENT.` → `WHO ISN'T MOVED BY EITHER?`

segments.voice: Arjuna's question is verse twenty-one, and he asks three things: the marks, the behavior, the way. Krishna answers with a portrait. Verse twenty-two: when light, activity and confusion come, this person doesn't hate them. When they go, doesn't long for them. Notice: the threads still show up. Even the person beyond the gunas has sleepy mornings and busy afternoons. The difference is the grip. Verse twenty-three: they sit like someone unconcerned, udasina, literally sitting above, not shaken by the gunas, knowing, it's just the threads moving. Verse twenty-four: the same in sorrow and happiness, resting in the self, a lump of clay, a stone and gold all the same to them. The same toward the pleasant and the unpleasant, steady, the same in blame and in praise of themselves. Verse twenty-five: the same in honor and dishonor, the same to friend and enemy. That person, Krishna says, has gone beyond the gunas. Gunatita. And then the answer to Arjuna's third question, how to get there. Verse twenty-six: the one who serves me with unwavering devotion goes beyond the three and becomes fit for Brahman. So the path beyond the threads isn't a technique for crushing them. In this chapter, it's bhakti, love. Verse twenty-seven closes: I am the ground of Brahman, of the deathless, of lasting dharma, and of perfect joy. This isn't indifference. It's the steadiness of someone whose center is somewhere the likes and comments can't reach. That's the word today: beyond the three.
screen: `THE THREADS STILL COME AND GO.` · `SITTING ABOVE, UNSHAKEN.` · `CLAY, STONE AND GOLD, THE SAME.` · `THE WAY BEYOND IS DEVOTION.` · then, large: `BEYOND THE THREE.`

segments.voice: Sit, and remember a recent word of praise. Let it land. Notice the lift in the chest. Now remember a recent word of blame. Let that land too. Notice the drop. Now, without pushing either away, see if you can sit a little above both, like someone watching weather from a hill. The lift and the drop still come. You're just not living inside them for a moment. The bell holds the time.
Gunatita, gone beyond the gunas. Gita fourteen: the one who has gone beyond the gunas doesn't hate them when they come or long for them when they go, and is the same in praise and blame.
Your line: the same in praise and blame. Today, when someone praises you or criticizes you, take one breath before you react, and let it pass through. Day two hundred nine.

screen: `DAY 209 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE TREE WITH ROOTS ABOVE.`

210.title: The tree with roots above (15.1–15.6)
210.hook: chapter fifteen opens with a sacred fig tree growing upside down
210.howItsDone: The peepal (ashvattha, sacred fig) is honored by Hindus: some water it, tie threads around it and walk around it; Gita 15 uses it as an image of the world, and some recite chapter fifteen on its own.

segments.voice: Yesterday: gunatita, beyond the three. The threads still come and go, but the one beyond them isn't gripped. Your line was the same in praise and blame. Did a word pass through you today? Now, a tree. Day two hundred ten.

A huge old peepal tree stands at the edge of a village square. Threads are tied around its trunk. Someone walks slow circles around it. Two old men sit in its shade and argue about cricket. Its heart-shaped leaves tremble in the slightest breeze. It's the sacred fig, the ashvattha. Now flip that tree over in your mind. Roots up in the sky. Branches hanging down, spreading all over the earth. That strange picture is how chapter fifteen begins.
screen: `THE OLD PEEPAL IN THE VILLAGE.` → `THREADS TIED AROUND ITS TRUNK.` → `NOW FLIP IT OVER.`

segments.voice: Verse one. They speak of an undying ashvattha tree with its roots above and its branches below. Its leaves are the Vedic hymns. Whoever knows this tree knows the Vedas. The Katha Upanishad describes the same eternal fig with its roots above. So what's the tree? Commentators read it as the whole world of change we live in, samsara, the round of birth and death. Its roots are above because it grows from the highest source. Verse two: its branches spread up and down, fed by the three gunas, and its buds are the objects of the senses. And some roots stretch downward too, into the human world, tangling us in action. That's why the tree feels so real: we're hanging in its branches, and the branches keep growing. Verse three is honest: its real shape can't be seen from here. Not its end, not its beginning, not what it stands on. And then the surprise. This huge, deep-rooted tree, Krishna says, cut it down with the strong axe of non-attachment. Asanga, not clinging. Not with violence, not by running away, but by letting go. Verse four: then seek that place from which no one returns, and take refuge in the first person, from whom this ancient flow came. Verse six says that place isn't lit by sun, moon or fire. It's my highest home. This week took us through the field, humility, the one light, the three threads, rajas, how they show up, and going beyond them. Today it all becomes one picture. That's the word: the tree with roots above.
screen: `ROOTS ABOVE, BRANCHES BELOW.` · `THE LEAVES ARE HYMNS.` · `THE AXE OF NOT CLINGING.` · `A HOME NO SUN LIGHTS.` · then, large: `THE TREE WITH ROOTS ABOVE.`

segments.voice: Sit, and picture yourself among the branches of a great tree. Each branch is something you hold on to: a plan, a worry, a person, a wish. Feel your grip on one of them. Now, without dropping anything, loosen the grip a little. That's the axe the Gita means: not clinging. Then let your attention travel up the trunk, toward the roots, toward the source, and rest there. The bell holds the time.
Ashvattha, the sacred fig. Gita fifteen: the world of change as an upside-down tree, rooted in the highest, cut with the axe of not clinging.
Your line: upside-down tree. Today, when you catch yourself gripping, a result, an argument, a phone, loosen one finger. That's the axe. Day two hundred ten.

original.note: Sanskrit: ashvattha, the sacred fig (peepal), Ficus religiosa; the upside-down tree of Gita 15.1.

trapdoor: what you thought: the upside-down tree is just a strange image.
what it means: it's the whole world of change, rooted in the highest source, and freedom comes by cutting it with not clinging.
what a scholar hears: the image echoes Katha Upanishad 2.3.1 (6.1); Shankara's commentary glosses ashvattha as 'what won't stand till tomorrow', a picture of impermanence.
